items.title: L6: Simple and compound interest
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Interest questions appear in numerical tests because they combine percentages with repeated steps. Simple interest is calculated on the original sum only: interest = principal × rate × years ÷ 100. A sum of £2,000 at 5% simple interest earns £100 each year, so £300 over three years. Compound interest is added to the balance each year, so the next year's interest is calculated on a larger sum. Use a multiplier: a balance with 4% added each year is multiplied by 1.04 every year, so after two years it is multiplied by 1.04 × 1.04 = 1.0816. Always check whether the question asks for the interest earned or the final balance, because the difference is the original sum. To find the original sum when you know the final compound balance, divide by the multiplier, not by one plus the total rate. To find a rate from simple interest, divide the interest by the principal and by the number of years. To find the time, divide the interest by the interest earned in one year. Loans work the same way: the amount repaid is the amount borrowed plus interest. Convert months to years before you multiply, so 18 months is 1.5 years. Over short periods the two methods give similar answers, but over longer periods compounding pulls ahead. Write the multiplier down and check whether the interest is annual, because a question may not say.

questions.prompt: A savings account pays 3.5% simple interest a year. How much interest does £4,000 earn in three years?
questions.hint: Simple interest: 4,000 × 0.035 × 3 = £420.

questions.prompt: £2,500 is invested at 4% compound interest, added once a year. What is the balance after two years?
£10,000 is held for three years at 5%. How much more is the closing balance if interest is compounded annually than if it is simple interest?
questions.hint: Compound balance is £11,576.25 and simple balance is £11,500, a difference of £76.25.

questions.prompt: A department's staff loan of £6,000 carries 8% simple interest a year. How much is repaid in total if it is cleared in full after 18 months?
questions.hint: 18 months is 1.5 years: 6,000 × 0.08 × 1.5 = 720 interest, so 6,720 in total.

questions.prompt: £8,000 earns £640 in simple interest over two years. What is the annual rate?
questions.hint: Interest per year is £320, and 320 ÷ 8,000 = 4%.

questions.prompt: Account A pays 4.2% simple interest and Account B pays 3.8% compound interest, each on £3,000 for five years. Which earns more, and by how much?

options.text: Account B, by £60
Account A, by £15.00
Account A, by £60
Account B, by £15.00

questions.hint: A earns £630; B earns 3,000 × (1.038^5 − 1), which is about £615.07.

questions.prompt: How many years does it take £2,000 to earn £500 at 5% simple interest?

options.text: 5 years
2.5 years
10 years
50 years

questions.hint: One year earns £100, and 500 ÷ 100 = 5 years.

questions.prompt: After two years at 5% compound interest, a balance stands at £4,410. What was the original deposit?

items.title: L6: Weighted averages and combined groups
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: A simple mean adds the values and divides by how many there are. When groups differ in size, you must use a weighted mean: multiply each group's mean by its size, add the totals, then divide by the combined size. If a group of 10 has a mean of 50 and a group of 30 has a mean of 70, the combined mean is (500 + 2,100) ÷ 40 = 65, not 60, because the larger group counts for more. A mean can also be worked backwards. The total of all values is the mean multiplied by the count, so a missing value is the required total minus the sum of the known values. Adding a new value changes a mean by the gap between the new value and the old mean, shared across the new count. Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the mean of two speeds. A journey made at two speeds over the same distance takes longer at the slower speed, so the average sits closer to the slower speed. Mixtures follow the same logic: the proportion of juice in a blend is the total juice divided by the total volume. In tender scoring, each criterion's score is multiplied by its percentage weight and the results are added. Check that weights add to 100% and that each weight is attached to the right criterion before you calculate.

questions.prompt: Team A has 12 staff with a mean test score of 70. Team B has 18 staff with a mean score of 80. What is the mean score across both teams?
The mean of five scores is 64. A sixth score of 88 is added. What is the new mean?
questions.hint: Total is 320, plus 88 is 408, and 408 ÷ 6 = 68.

questions.prompt: Sam drives 60 miles to a meeting at 30 mph and returns by the same route at 60 mph. What is the average speed for the whole journey?

options.text: 40 mph
36 mph
45 mph
50 mph

questions.hint: 120 miles takes 2 + 1 = 3 hours, and 120 ÷ 3 = 40 mph.

questions.prompt: The mean of four numbers is 15. Three of them are 9, 14 and 21. What is the fourth?
questions.hint: The total is 60 and the known three add to 44, leaving 16.

questions.prompt: A class of 21 has a mean mark of 60. One student who scored 100 leaves. What is the mean of the remaining 20?
3 litres of drink containing 20% juice are mixed with 2 litres containing 45% juice. What percentage of the blend is juice?
questions.hint: Juice is 0.6 + 0.9 = 1.5 litres out of 5 litres, which is 30%.

questions.prompt: A tender is scored 50% on price, 30% on quality and 20% on delivery. A bidder scores 8, 6 and 9 out of 10 respectively. What is the weighted score?
Over four weeks, a contractor averages 36 hours a week. The first three weeks were 35, 38 and 32 hours. How many hours were worked in week four?
questions.hint: The total is 144 and the first three weeks give 105, so 144 − 105 = 39.

items.title: L6: Tables, shares and percentage points
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Many numerical questions give a short table in the text and ask for a change or a share. The percentage change is the difference divided by the starting figure, then multiplied by 100. A rise from 8,400 to 9,660 is 1,260 ÷ 8,400 = 15%. Dividing by the new figure is the commonest mistake. A share is a part divided by the whole. When a question gives a percentage of a total, convert it to a number first, because the totals may change from year to year. A percentage point is the arithmetic gap between two percentages, while a percentage change compares that gap to the starting percentage. Satisfaction rising from 40% to 50% is 10 percentage points but a 25% relative increase. Index numbers are a series scaled so that one year equals 100. A change between two later years is found by comparing the index values, not by subtracting from 100. A fall of 12% leaves 88% of the original, so the original is the new figure divided by 0.88, not the new figure plus 12%. When several budget lines move by different percentages, work out each line separately, then add. Compare rates per head when groups differ in size, because totals alone mislead. Always ask which figure is the base for each percentage.

questions.prompt: Claims received rose from 8,400 in 2022 to 9,660 in 2023. By what percentage did they rise?
In 2021, 62% of 5,000 applications were made online. In 2023, 78% of 6,500 were. By what percentage did the number of online applications rise?
questions.hint: Online applications went from 3,100 to 5,070, a rise of 1,970 ÷ 3,100 = 63.5%.

questions.prompt: Staff numbers between 2022 and 2024: Leeds 400 to 450, Cardiff 240 to 252, Glasgow 80 to 100. Which office saw the biggest percentage rise?

options.text: Leeds, 50%
Glasgow, 20%
Glasgow, 25%
Leeds, 12.5%

questions.hint: Glasgow rose by 20 on a base of 80, which is 25%, more than Leeds at 12.5%.

questions.prompt: Satisfaction in a survey rose from 54% to 63%. Which description is accurate?

options.text: A rise of 9 percentage points, a relative increase of 9%
A rise of about 17 percentage points, a relative increase of 9%
A rise of 9 percentage points, a relative increase of about 14%
A rise of 9 percentage points, a relative increase of about 17%

questions.hint: The gap is 9 points, and 9 ÷ 54 is about 16.7%.

questions.prompt: After a 12% fall, a figure stands at 4,400. What was it before the fall?
questions.hint: The new figure is 88% of the original, so 4,400 ÷ 0.88 = 5,000.

questions.prompt: A £2.4m budget splits as staffing 55%, IT 20%, premises 15% and other 10%. Staffing rises 5% and IT is cut 10%; the other lines are unchanged. What is the new total?
questions.hint: Staffing is 1.386, IT is 0.432, premises 0.36 and other 0.24, which total 2.418.

questions.prompt: Department X handles 18,000 cases with 120 staff. Department Y handles 14,400 cases with 90 staff. By what percentage is Y's caseload per member of staff higher than X's?
questions.hint: X handles 150 each and Y handles 160 each, and 10 ÷ 150 is about 6.7%.

questions.prompt: An index of waiting times was 100 in 2019, 108 in 2021 and 126 in 2023. By what percentage did waiting times rise between 2021 and 2023?
questions.hint: The gap is 18, and 18 ÷ 108 is about 16.7%.

items.title: L6: Currency conversion with fees and rates
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Currency questions test whether you multiply or divide by the exchange rate. If £1 buys €1.15, then to change pounds into euros you multiply by 1.15, and to change euros into pounds you divide by 1.15. A quick check helps: a pound buys more than one euro, so a euro price should become a smaller sterling figure. Fees come in several forms. A percentage commission is deducted from the amount before or after conversion, so read which. A flat fee is subtracted once. When both apply, take them in the order the question states. Buying and selling rates differ: a bureau sells foreign money at one rate and buys it back at a worse one, and the gap is its margin. To compare prices in two countries, convert both to the same currency and include any tax that is added at the till. VAT in the UK is already part of a shelf price, whereas some countries add sales tax at the till. A change in the rate alters the sterling cost of a foreign invoice: if the pound weakens from €1.20 to €1.08, a €600 bill costs more in sterling. Percentage changes in an exchange rate are not the same as percentage changes in the cost, so work out the sterling amounts and compare them. Keep working to at least two decimal places until the final answer.

questions.prompt: The rate is £1 = €1.15. A hotel bill is €276. What is it in pounds?
questions.hint: Divide euros by the rate: 276 ÷ 1.15 = £240.

questions.prompt: A bureau charges 2% commission on the sterling amount before converting at £1 = $1.30. How many dollars do you get for £500?
Jo buys euros at £1 = €1.14 with £400, then sells them all back later at £1 = €1.20. How much does she lose?
questions.hint: She gets 456 euros, and 456 ÷ 1.20 = £380 back, a loss of £20.

questions.prompt: A coat costs £84 in the UK including 20% VAT. In the US it costs $96 before 8% sales tax, and £1 = $1.25. Which is cheaper, and by how much?

options.text: The UK coat, by £1.06
The US coat, by £1.06
The UK coat, by £19.68
The US coat, by £7.20

questions.hint: US price with tax is $103.68, which is £82.94 at 1.25, so £1.06 cheaper.

questions.prompt: A subsistence allowance is €55 a day for 6 days. The rate is £1 = €1.10. What is the allowance in pounds?
questions.hint: The total is €330, and 330 ÷ 1.10 = £300.

questions.prompt: A supplier invoice for €600 cost £500 when £1 = €1.20. The pound falls to £1 = €1.08. By what percentage does the sterling cost rise?
A bureau charges £3 plus 1.5% of the amount, deducted before converting at £1 = €1.10. How many euros do you get for £280?
Fuel in Spain is €1.62 a litre. In the UK it is 142.5p a litre. If £1 = €1.20, which is cheaper per litre, and by how much?

options.text: Spain, by 7.5p
Spain, by 19.5p
The UK, by 19.5p
The UK, by 7.5p

items.title: L6: Ratios, rates and proportion
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Ratio questions test whether you can turn parts into amounts and back again. To share a sum in a ratio, add the parts, divide the sum by that total to find one part, then multiply. Sharing £3,150 in the ratio 2:3:4 means 9 parts of £350 each. When a ratio changes because people move between groups, recalculate the actual numbers first and then rebuild the ratio. Direct proportion means doubling one quantity doubles the other, as with cost and quantity. Inverse proportion means that doubling the workers halves the time, so multiply workers by days to find the constant. Combined rates add: if one machine processes 120 forms an hour and another 90, together they process 210 an hour. Do not average the rates. Where a question changes two things, such as the number of scanners and the time, scale each in turn, or find a rate per scanner per minute. Tiered pricing charges one rate for the first block and a different rate beyond it, so cost each block separately. Unit prices compare packs of different size: divide price by quantity, then compare, rounding only at the end. A difference of a penny per item can matter over thousands of items. Always check that units match, such as hours and minutes, before you divide.

questions.prompt: £3,150 is shared in the ratio 2:3:4. What is the largest share?
questions.hint: There are 9 parts of £350, and 4 parts is £1,400.

questions.prompt: Machine A processes 120 forms an hour and Machine B processes 90. Working together, how long do they take to process 2,520 forms?

options.text: 24 hours
28 hours
12 hours
21 hours

questions.hint: Together they process 210 an hour, and 2,520 ÷ 210 = 12.

questions.prompt: Six staff clear a backlog in 15 days. How long would 9 staff take at the same pace?

options.text: 10 days
12 days
9 days
22.5 days

questions.hint: 6 × 15 = 90 staff-days, and 90 ÷ 9 = 10.

questions.prompt: The ratio of full-time to part-time staff is 5:3 in a team of 96. Twelve part-time staff move to full-time contracts. What is the new ratio of full-time to part-time?
questions.hint: Before: 60 and 36. After: 72 and 24, which simplifies to 3:1.

questions.prompt: Printing costs 4.5p a page for the first 2,000 pages and 3p a page beyond that. What is the cost of 3,500 pages?
Four scanners scan 600 pages in 25 minutes. How many pages would 6 scanners scan in 40 minutes at the same rate?
questions.hint: Each scanner does 6 pages a minute, and 6 × 6 × 40 = 1,440.

questions.prompt: A 24-pack of pens costs £7.20 and a 40-pack costs £11.60. Which is cheaper per pen?

options.text: Neither, both cost 30p a pen
The 40-pack, by 1p a pen
The 24-pack, by 1p a pen
The 40-pack, by 4p a pen

questions.prompt: A £5,400 bonus pool is shared in proportion to hours worked: Asha 120, Ben 100, Chloe 50. How much does Ben receive?
questions.hint: Total hours are 270, so each hour is worth £20 and Ben gets 100 × 20.

items.title: L6: Verdicts when a passage sets rules and exceptions
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Verbal reasoning passages often set out a rule, an exception to the rule, and a condition for the exception. The verdict you give must rest only on the words of the passage. Method: first, underline the rule, the exception and any numbers. Second, test the statement against each part. Third, decide whether the passage proves it (True), contradicts it (False) or leaves it open (Cannot say). Worked example: a passage says that a visitor pass is issued to anyone with a booked appointment, except on public holidays, when only staff may enter. A statement says that a visitor with a booking can enter on Christmas Day. The exception removes visitor entry on public holidays, so the verdict is False. Another trap is the reverse of a rule. 'Only trained staff may enter' does not tell you that every person who entered was trained, because people can break rules. Equally, a rule that applies to amounts 'over £50,000' does not cover exactly £50,000, and not needing approval does not mean approval was not given. Watch quantifiers such as 'at least', 'most', 'all' and 'some', and compare percentages and fractions carefully before choosing a verdict.

questions.prompt: "Staff may work from home for up to three days a week, unless their manager has agreed in writing that the role needs more office time. Staff in the first six months of a new post must attend the office on at least four of their five working days." Statement: "A member of staff in the first six months of a new post may work from home for three days a week." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not define a new post
True: the three-day limit applies to all staff
Cannot say: the manager's written agreement could allow it
False: they must attend at least four of five days, leaving one day at home

questions.hint: The six-month rule overrides the general limit.

questions.prompt: "Grants over £50,000 need approval from the finance director. The finance director approved every grant awarded last quarter that exceeded £50,000. Three grants of exactly £50,000 were also awarded." Statement: "The finance director approved the three grants of exactly £50,000." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: exactly £50,000 is not over the threshold, and approval is not mentioned
False: those grants did not need approval, so they were not approved
True: all grants need the director's approval
Cannot say: the passage does not give the total value of grants

questions.hint: Not needing approval does not mean approval was withheld.

questions.prompt: "A helpline answered 92% of calls within 60 seconds in March, against a target of 90%. In April the figure was 88%. Staffing was unchanged between the two months." Statement: "The fall in April was caused by a rise in call volumes." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not give April's target
Cannot say: the passage gives no cause, only that staffing was unchanged
True: staffing was unchanged, so call volumes must have risen
False: staffing was unchanged, so nothing could have changed

questions.hint: Other causes, such as longer calls or absence, are possible.

questions.prompt: "Of the 240 staff in a unit, 60% completed an optional course. Of those who completed it, three quarters passed the final assessment, and every pass was awarded a certificate." Statement: "108 members of the unit received a certificate." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: only the 144 who completed the course received certificates
Cannot say: some staff may have been awarded certificates without passing
True: 60% of 240 is 144, and three quarters of 144 is 108
False: three quarters of 240 is 180

questions.prompt: "A review found that complaints rose by 14% over the year, while the number of transactions processed rose by 30%. The review recommended no change to the complaints procedure." Statement: "The number of complaints per transaction fell over the year." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the actual numbers of complaints are not given
True: complaints grew more slowly than transactions, so there were fewer per transaction
False: the number of complaints rose over the year
Cannot say: the reason for the review's recommendation is not given

questions.hint: 1.14 ÷ 1.30 is less than 1, so the rate fell whatever the starting numbers.

questions.prompt: "Only staff who have completed security training may enter Room 4. Dev has entered Room 4 several times this month." Statement: "Dev has completed security training." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage gives a rule but not whether Dev followed it
False: Dev has entered more than once, which suggests the rule is not enforced
True: only trained staff may enter, so Dev must be trained
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long the training takes

questions.hint: A rule states what is allowed, not what has happened.

questions.prompt: "Expenses claims must be submitted within 28 days of travel. Late claims are paid only if the claimant's manager confirms a valid reason in writing. Ravi travelled on 3 March and submitted a claim on 5 April. His manager has declined to confirm any reason." Statement: "Ravi's claim will be paid." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: the claim was submitted in the same financial year
Cannot say: the passage does not say how much the claim is for
False: it was submitted 33 days after travel with no confirmation from his manager
Cannot say: the passage does not say whether late claims are ever paid

questions.hint: 3 March to 5 April is 33 days, and the late-claim condition is not met.

questions.prompt: "A consultation attracted 1,800 responses. Of these, 1,260 supported the proposal, 360 opposed it and the rest expressed no view. The department says the proposal has strong public support." Statement: "A majority of those who responded supported the proposal." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: 360 respondents opposed the proposal
Cannot say: the number who expressed no view is not given
Cannot say: respondents may not represent the public as a whole
True: 1,260 is 70% of the 1,800 responses

questions.hint: The statement is about respondents only, and 1,260 ÷ 1,800 = 70%.

items.title: L6: Verdicts when evidence is statistical or causal
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Passages that contain statistics are designed to tempt you into reading more into them than they say. Keep these checks in mind. Correlation is not causation: two things appearing together does not show that one caused the other. Averages can hide extremes: if the mean payment is £3,000, then at least one payment is £3,000 or more, but you cannot say how the rest are spread. A rate and a number are different things: five out of eight is 62.5%, which is higher than 40 out of 100, even though 40 is the bigger number. A percentage of a sample says nothing certain about the whole population, particularly if only some of the people asked chose to reply. Past trends do not prove future trends, so a passage that reports a fall does not show the fall will continue. Percentage changes compare to the starting figure, so a drop from £4.2m to £3.5m is a fall of £0.7m, which is one sixth of £4.2m, not one fifth. Worked example: a passage says that the success rate of appeals rose from 25% to 30%. A statement says that more appeals succeeded. You cannot say, because the number of appeals is not given. Read the exact words, check what is being compared, then decide.

questions.prompt: "Offices with plants on desks reported higher staff satisfaction than offices without them. The survey covered 40 offices." Statement: "Putting plants in an office raises staff satisfaction." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the survey shows an association but not that plants caused the difference
Cannot say: the passage does not say how satisfaction was measured
True: offices with plants scored higher
False: 40 offices is too small a sample to show anything

questions.hint: Association alone does not establish cause.

questions.prompt: "Last year 5 of the 8 appeals heard by a tribunal succeeded. This year 40 of 100 appeals succeeded." Statement: "The success rate was higher last year than this year." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: more appeals succeeded this year
Cannot say: the number of appeals differs between the years
True: 5 out of 8 is 62.5%, compared with 40%
Cannot say: the tribunal's membership may have changed

questions.hint: Compare rates, not totals.

questions.prompt: "Since a new booking system was introduced in January, the average wait for an appointment has fallen from 12 days to 9 days." Statement: "Waiting times will continue to fall." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say which month the figures cover
True: the fall shows the system works
False: a fall from 12 to 9 days cannot continue indefinitely
Cannot say: the passage describes a past change and does not predict the future

questions.hint: A past trend does not show what will happen next.

questions.prompt: "An agency employs 500 staff, of whom 35% work in the north. Of its 150 managers, a fifth work in the north." Statement: "More than half of the staff in the north are managers." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say how many staff are managers
False: 175 staff work in the north and only 30 managers do
True: managers are the largest group in the north
Cannot say: managers may also be counted among the 500 staff

questions.hint: 30 out of 175 is well under half.

questions.prompt: "A report states that fraud losses fell from £4.2m to £3.5m. It does not give the number of cases." Statement: "Fraud losses fell by one sixth." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say why losses fell
True: the fall of £0.7m is one sixth of £4.2m
False: the fall is one fifth
Cannot say: the number of cases is not given

questions.prompt: "Three quarters of a team's reports are checked by a second reader, and the team produced 80 reports last month." Statement: "At least 60 reports were checked by a second reader last month." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: three quarters of 80 is 40
Cannot say: the passage does not say if the rate applied last month
True: three quarters of 80 is 60
Cannot say: the passage does not say which reports were checked

questions.prompt: "A union survey found that 62% of members who replied were satisfied with a pay offer. The survey went to all members and 25% replied." Statement: "Most union members are satisfied with the pay offer." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: only 25% of members replied
True: 62% is a majority
Cannot say: the passage does not say when the survey was sent
Cannot say: only a quarter replied, and those who did may not be typical

questions.hint: A low response rate means the replies may not represent all members.

questions.prompt: "A scheme has paid out £6m to 2,000 claimants. No claimant received more than £9,000." Statement: "At least one claimant received £3,000 or more." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: the mean is £3,000, so at least one payment is £3,000 or more
Cannot say: the payments may not have been equal
Cannot say: the minimum payment is not given
False: the maximum is £9,000, so most payments were low

questions.hint: If every payment were below £3,000 the total would be below £6m.

items.title: L6: Which conclusion follows from the premises
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Deductive questions give premises and ask which conclusion must be true. The answer must follow with certainty, not just look likely. Learn the common patterns. 'All A are B' means every A is a B, but it does not mean every B is an A. 'Some A are B' means at least one, and does not say that the rest are not. 'No A are B' is symmetrical: no B are A either. A conditional 'If P then Q' tells you two safe things: if P is true then Q is true, and if Q is false then P is false. It does not tell you that Q being true makes P true, nor that P being false makes Q false. Chains of conditionals link up: if P gives Q, and Q gives R, then P gives R. An 'either … or' statement means that if one option is false the other is true. For ordering puzzles, write the relations as short lines and join them. For overlapping groups, use the rule: total = group one + group two − both + neither. Worked example: all analysts have security clearance, and Ayo is an analyst. Ayo has clearance follows. 'Everyone with clearance is an analyst' does not follow. Treat each answer option as a claim to test, and eliminate those that go beyond the premises.

questions.prompt: All grade 7 staff have completed the leadership module. Some staff who have completed the module work in Policy. Priya is a grade 7. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Everyone who has completed the module must be a grade 7
Priya works in Policy
All Policy staff are grade 7
Priya has completed the leadership module

questions.hint: The first premise applies to every grade 7, including Priya.

questions.prompt: No temporary staff have access to the payroll system. Everyone in the Payments team has access to the payroll system. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Only the Payments team has access to payroll
Nobody in the Payments team is temporary staff
All permanent staff have access to payroll
Some permanent staff are not in the Payments team

questions.hint: Payments staff have access, and temporary staff cannot, so they are not the same people.

questions.prompt: If the report is late, the minister is briefed in person. The minister was not briefed in person. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The report was not late
The report was late but the briefing was missed
The minister is only briefed in person when a report is late
Nothing can be concluded about the report

questions.hint: If the consequence is false, the condition must be false.

questions.prompt: Amir finished before Beth. Chen finished after Beth. Dana finished before Amir. Which is the order from first to last?

options.text: Amir, Dana, Beth, Chen
Dana, Beth, Amir, Chen
Dana, Amir, Beth, Chen
Dana, Amir, Chen, Beth

questions.hint: Dana < Amir < Beth < Chen.

questions.prompt: Every complaint received is logged. Some logged complaints are escalated. No escalated complaint is closed within a day. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Some logged complaints are not closed within a day
Not one complaint is ever closed within a day
Some complaints received are not logged
All logged complaints are escalated

questions.hint: The escalated ones are logged and none of them closes within a day.

questions.prompt: If the budget is approved, recruitment starts in June. If recruitment starts in June, new staff are in post by September. New staff were not in post by September. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The budget was approved but recruitment was slow
Recruitment started in June but staff left
The budget was not approved
Nothing can be concluded about the budget

questions.hint: Reverse the chain: no staff by September means no June start, which means no approval.

questions.prompt: Either the audit finds an error or the accounts are signed off this week. The accounts were not signed off this week. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The audit has not yet been carried out
The audit found an error
The accounts will be signed off next week
The audit found no error

questions.hint: If one alternative fails, the other holds.

questions.prompt: In a group of 30 staff, 18 speak Welsh, 12 speak French and 5 speak both. How many speak neither language?
questions.hint: 18 + 12 − 5 = 25 speak at least one, leaving 5.

items.title: L6: Strengthening and weakening an argument
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some verbal questions give a short argument and ask which extra fact would strengthen or weaken it. An argument has evidence, a conclusion, and a link between them. Strengthening evidence closes a gap in the link, for example by showing the evidence cannot be explained in another way. Weakening evidence opens a gap: it supplies another explanation, shows the sample is unrepresentative, or shows the measure has changed. Method: first, state the conclusion in your own words. Second, ask what else could explain the evidence. Third, check each option and ask whether it makes the conclusion more or less likely. Options that are merely about the same topic, or that restate the evidence, do little. Worked example: a department fits quieter printers and sickness absence falls, so the printers cut absence. A fact that absence fell across all departments for the same period weakens the claim, because something else may have caused the fall. A fact that a comparable department without the printers saw no fall strengthens it, because that comparison rules out a general cause. Good tests are comparisons, random allocation, consistent measurement and longer time periods. Be careful to answer the question actually asked: weaken, or strengthen.

questions.prompt: "A department introduced free fruit in its offices and sickness absence fell by 10% over the next year, so free fruit reduces sickness absence." Which fact most weakens this argument?

options.text: Some staff already ate fruit at their desks before the scheme began
Absence across the Civil Service fell by 10%
The department has 2,000 staff
The fruit was popular with staff and was supplied by a local firm

questions.hint: A general fall points to another cause.

questions.prompt: "The new application form should reduce errors, because a trial found that 3% of forms contained errors compared with 9% before." Which fact most strengthens this argument?

options.text: Errors on the old form had been falling slowly for several years before the trial
The new form is shorter than the old form and has clearer instructions
Trial participants said they preferred the new form because it was easy to fill in
Participants were randomly given the new or the old form, and the new form had fewer errors

questions.hint: Random allocation rules out differences between the groups.

questions.prompt: "Closing the small Exeter office would save money because it has the highest cost per member of staff." Which fact most weakens this argument?

options.text: Relocation and lease costs would exceed the saving for the first three years
The office has the lowest number of visitors
The Exeter office is the oldest building in the department and needs repairs
Most staff in the Exeter office live within walking distance

questions.hint: The conclusion is about saving money, so costs that cancel the saving matter most.

questions.prompt: "A survey of 50 people at a conference on road safety found that 90% support a new tax on fuel, so the public supports the tax." Which fact most weakens this argument?

options.text: The survey took about ten minutes to complete at the venue
Some respondents were visitors from overseas who answered by email
The conference was organised by a campaign group that lobbies for the tax
The tax would apply to all fuel types

questions.hint: The sample was probably not representative of the public.

questions.prompt: "Opening on Saturday mornings increased applications, because applications from people in full-time work rose most in the months after the change." Which fact most strengthens this argument?

options.text: The service launched a modern website at the start of the year
Applications from part-time workers also rose over the same months
Saturday opening costs more per hour than weekday opening
Nothing else changed in that period, and applications from that group had been flat before

questions.hint: Ruling out other changes and showing a flat earlier trend supports the claim.

questions.prompt: "Since callbacks were introduced, abandoned calls fell from 12% to 6%, so callbacks improved the service." Which fact most weakens this argument?

options.text: Callbacks usually take place within two hours of the request
Calls requesting a callback are now recorded as answered calls
The helpline is open from 8am
Some callers prefer to wait on hold rather than receive a call

questions.hint: A change in how calls are counted could explain the fall without any change in service.

questions.prompt: "The department should train staff in-house rather than buy courses, because in-house training costs £400 a head compared with £650." Which fact most strengthens this argument?

options.text: In-house courses achieve pass rates similar to bought-in courses
Bought-in courses are well regarded by other departments
Some staff prefer a classroom setting
In-house trainers are paid on a standard grade

questions.hint: Comparable results confirm that cost is the deciding difference.

questions.prompt: "Fewer prosecutions were brought this year, so the number of offences fell." Which fact most weakens this argument?

options.text: Offences also fell in neighbouring countries
Prosecutions are usually reported in the local press
The prosecuting body lost a fifth of its staff this year
Offences are rising in most categories

questions.hint: Fewer prosecutions may simply reflect reduced capacity.

items.title: L6: Spotting the assumption behind an argument
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: An assumption is an unstated step that an argument needs in order to work. If the assumption were false, the conclusion would not follow. To find one, state the evidence and the conclusion and ask what must also be true for the first to lead to the second. The assumption is usually a bridge: that a trend will continue, that one thing caused another, that a sample represents a group, or that a measure captures what matters. Distinguish an assumption from a stated fact and from something merely helpful. A good test is the negation test: negate the option, and if the argument collapses, it was a necessary assumption. Worked example: 'The new portal lets users check progress online, so it will cut calls.' The argument assumes that people who currently phone to check progress would use the portal instead. If they would not, calls would not fall. 'The portal was cheap to build' is not needed for the conclusion. Be careful with options that are too strong, such as 'all users', when the argument needs only that enough users change behaviour. Options that bring in a new topic do not support the specific step in the argument.

questions.prompt: "The team should adopt flexible hours, because staff who work flexibly are more productive." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: The team's productivity would respond to flexible hours as that of the staff compared did
All staff in the team would like to work flexibly if they were asked
Staff who are productive always prefer to have flexibility
Flexible hours are cheaper to administer than fixed hours for managers

questions.hint: The argument moves from other staff to this team.

questions.prompt: "The new portal lets people check the progress of their claim online, so it will reduce calls to the helpline." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: Calls to check progress are the cheapest type of call
Many people who now phone to check progress would use the portal instead
The portal will cost less than the helpline
The portal has been tested by an outside supplier

questions.hint: Calls only fall if callers change behaviour.

questions.prompt: "Only 40% of staff attended the briefing, so the department's communication is poor." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: The briefing lasted longer than usual and covered several topics
Staff who missed the briefing were on leave or off sick that day
Attendance at the briefing is a fair measure of how well the department communicates
All staff have been invited to every briefing

questions.hint: Attendance is treated as a measure of communication quality.

questions.prompt: "We should raise the inspection rate, because inspected firms commit fewer breaches." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: Every firm will be inspected at the same rate
Inspectors are paid less than the penalties collected
Breaches are more costly than inspections
Inspection itself reduces breaches, rather than lower-risk firms being the ones inspected

questions.hint: It assumes a causal link from inspection to compliance.

questions.prompt: "The cost of the scheme rose by 20% last year, so it now offers worse value for money." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: The scheme is the department's largest
The scheme was already good value before the rise in cost
The cost of other schemes in the department did not rise
The benefits delivered did not rise by at least as much as the cost

questions.hint: Value for money compares cost with benefit.

questions.prompt: "A staff survey had a response rate of only 30%, so its results should be ignored." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: The people who did not respond hold different views from those who did
The survey asked too many questions and took too long to finish
Staff are rarely honest in surveys, whatever the response rate
A response rate of 30% is the lowest ever recorded

questions.hint: If non-responders were similar, a low rate would matter less.

questions.prompt: "Data collected using public money should be published, so the department should publish its call-centre records." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: Members of the public have asked to see the records
Other departments already publish similar records online
The records were publicly funded and contain nothing confidential
Publishing would be quick and inexpensive for the department

questions.hint: The rule is applied to this data, so its fit and any limits matter.

questions.prompt: "The last two heads of the unit each left within a year, so the new head will not stay long." Which assumption does the argument depend on?

options.text: Heads of other units stay for many years
The new head is likely to face the same pressures or conditions as the previous two
The new head was hired on a short fixed-term contract
The new head wants to leave

questions.hint: The prediction assumes the past pattern will repeat.

items.title: L6: Conflicts of interest, gifts and hospitality
items.body: The Civil Service Code requires you not to misuse your official position, not to accept gifts or hospitality that might reasonably be seen to compromise your personal judgement or integrity, and not to let private interests conflict with public duties. A conflict of interest exists when a private interest, such as a family tie, a financial stake or an outside job, could influence, or appear to influence, your decisions. The test is not whether you would actually be biased but whether a fair observer might think you could be. The standard response is to declare the interest early to your line manager, who decides whether you should step back from the decision, and to record it in the register your department keeps. Departments usually have a policy on gifts and hospitality: low-value items may be accepted or declined with thanks, anything of significant value is usually refused or reported, and offers from suppliers during a procurement or around a contract decision are treated with particular care. Offering or taking a bribe is a criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010. Outside jobs usually need approval before you accept them. Worked example: you are asked to help score tenders, and a bidder is run by your cousin. You tell your manager before you see any scores, so a different scorer can be found. Avoid answers that hide the interest, that rely on your own confidence in being fair, or that tidy the matter away afterwards.

questions.prompt: After a tender decision, a supplier sends a large hamper to your team. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your line manager, record the offer as the gifts policy requires, and usually decline or return it
Share the hamper out among the team, since the contract decision has already been made and cannot be affected
Keep it quietly yourself, as the contract has been awarded and nobody will mind
Give the hamper to charity without telling anyone, so that nobody in the team benefits personally

questions.hint: Gifts around a contract decision are declared and handled under the policy, not disposed of privately.

questions.prompt: You are evaluating bids for a contract and find that your brother's company is one of the bidders. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Score all bids carefully and fairly, as you know you can stay objective
Mention it to a colleague informally and carry on scoring
Score your brother's bid slightly lower to avoid any bias in his favour
Tell your manager at once and step back from evaluating the bids

questions.hint: The risk is the appearance of bias, so the decision belongs to your manager.

questions.prompt: A charity that your team funds offers you a free lunch in return for a short talk. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Decline politely and suggest the charity speaks to your manager
Ask your manager whether you may accept
Accept without telling anyone, since the lunch is only a sandwich
Check the gifts and hospitality policy before replying

questions.hint: Accepting from an organisation you fund without disclosure risks the appearance of influence.

questions.prompt: You are offered a paid evening role advising a company that sells to your department. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Accept the role, then mention it to your manager at your next performance review
Disclose the offer to your line manager and wait for approval before accepting
Decline to say who the client is, since your evenings are a private matter
Accept, provided the work is done outside office hours and not on department equipment

questions.hint: Outside work needs approval, particularly when the employer is a supplier.

questions.prompt: You have been named on an interview panel and learn that a close friend has applied. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the recruiting manager and ask to be removed from the panel
Say nothing, as you will judge the candidates on the evidence
Stay on the panel but score your friend last, to be on the safe side
Stay on the panel and ask other members to check your scores

questions.hint: Recruitment must be on merit and be seen to be, so the conflict is declared.

questions.prompt: You own shares in a company that a policy you are drafting would affect. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Carry on as normal, since a small shareholding would not change your advice
Sell the shares immediately and carry on with the drafting without telling anyone
Declare the shareholding to your manager, who can decide whether you should stay on the work
Ask a colleague to review your draft afterwards so that the advice is balanced

questions.hint: Your manager decides how to manage the conflict, once informed.

questions.prompt: While a contract renewal is pending, a supplier offers your team free tickets to a sporting final. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Accept, but only for tickets that the whole team shares
Politely decline and tell your manager about the offer so it can be recorded
Accept and pay for your own food and drink at the event
Accept the tickets after the renewal decision has been made

questions.hint: The timing makes any acceptance look like an inducement.

questions.prompt: A colleague confides that they hold a small stake in a contractor you are about to appoint, and asks you to keep it quiet. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Explain that the interest should be declared to the manager
Tell them you cannot promise confidentiality about a conflict
Offer to go with them to speak to the manager
Agree to say nothing, since the stake is small

questions.hint: Concealing an interest in a procurement undermines fairness, however small the stake.

questions.prompt: A supplier's account manager offers you a personal discount at their shop because you work with their company. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Accept, but do not use it to buy anything for the office
Ask for the offer in writing so there is a record of it
Decline the offer and mention it to your manager, as it relates to your official role
Accept, since all customers are offered discounts at times

questions.hint: A benefit offered because of your role is treated as a gift.

items.title: L6: Protecting personal data in daily work
items.source: UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018 and ICO guidance
items.body: Civil servants handle personal data about the public and colleagues, and the law expects it to be used only for the purpose it was collected, kept secure, and shared only with people who have a legitimate need. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) regulates this. Common risks include sending an email to the wrong recipient, leaving a laptop or papers on public transport, saving files where anyone can open them, and looking up records out of curiosity or for a friend. If something goes wrong, tell your line manager and the data protection or security team straight away, because the organisation may have to report a personal data breach to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, where the breach is likely to risk people's rights. You do not decide that alone, and you should not wait to find out whether harm occurs. Individuals also have a right to ask for their data, called a subject access request, and organisations normally have one month to reply, so these requests should be passed to the right team promptly. Press questions go to the press office. Worked example: you email a spreadsheet to the wrong external address. You report it immediately, say what was sent, and try to recall it if you can. You do not quietly ask the recipient to delete it and hope. Avoid options that hide the problem, delay reporting, or tamper with evidence.

questions.prompt: You email a spreadsheet of claimants' details to the wrong external address. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the recipient to delete it and not mention the matter again to anyone
Email the affected claimants yourself with an apology, before anyone else is told
Wait a day or two to see whether the recipient replies to the email
Tell your manager and the data protection team straight away, and try to recall the email

questions.hint: A prompt report lets the organisation assess and, if required, notify the ICO within 72 hours.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks for a claimant's home address so they can send a personal card. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Decline politely, explaining that the data may only be used for official purposes
Give it, but ask them to delete it straight after they have used it
Give it, as the colleague works for the same department and can be trusted
Give it only if the claimant's file is marked as low risk

questions.hint: Using data for a personal purpose is not what it was collected for.

questions.prompt: You leave your encrypted work laptop on a train. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Buy a replacement and report it at the next team meeting
Report the loss at once to IT security and your manager, despite encryption
Wait until the next day in case someone hands it in to the station
Report it only if you know you stored personal data on it

questions.hint: Loss must be reported promptly so risk can be assessed, whatever protection the device has.

questions.prompt: A written request arrives from a member of the public asking to see all the information held about them. A colleague says it can wait until the claimant chases. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reply informally to say the department will look into it soon
Pass it to the data protection team at once, as the one-month limit has started
Wait for the claimant to send proof of identity again
Hold it until you have gathered all the records yourself and checked them

questions.hint: The clock runs from receipt, and specialist handling is needed.

questions.prompt: You find a folder of claimant details saved on a shared drive that anyone in the department can open. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Copy it to your own private area of the drive to keep it safe
Email the whole team to ask who saved it there and why
Delete the whole folder immediately to remove the risk
Report it to the owner and security team so access can be restricted

questions.hint: Deleting could destroy evidence and records, and the owner needs to know.

questions.prompt: You discover a data loss on Friday evening, when most of your team has left. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Write down what you know so the details are clear
Phone the out-of-hours security contact
Leave it until Monday morning, when the whole team is back at work
Email your manager with the facts straight away

questions.hint: The 72-hour window continues over the weekend.

questions.prompt: You are working from home and have a printed document containing claimants' details. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Follow the department's guidance on printing and storage, and ask your manager if unsure
Print only the pages you need and put them in the household bin at the end of the week
Use your home printer, since you work in a private space and live alone, then shred the copy
Photograph the pages on your phone as a backup

questions.hint: Handling rules apply wherever you work, and unclear cases are raised with your manager.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to check on the department's system whether an address is valid. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Explain that you cannot access records for personal reasons
Look it up, as you would only confirm yes or no
Decline, and tell your manager if the friend keeps asking
Suggest the friend contacts the department through the official route

questions.hint: Accessing data without a work reason is misuse, even if little is revealed.

questions.prompt: A journalist phones you asking whether the department has lost claimants' data. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say you cannot comment and refer the journalist to the press office
Offer to answer questions if the journalist agrees not to name you or the team
Say there has been no loss, to avoid causing alarm among claimants
Confirm that an incident is being investigated, without giving further details

questions.hint: Media enquiries go through the press office, which has the facts and authority.

items.title: L6: Raising a concern and reporting wrongdoing
items.source: The Civil Service Code and Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Code says that if you become aware of actions by others that you believe are improper, illegal, unethical or a danger to the public, you should report it. Your first route is usually your line manager or another senior manager. Many departments also have a nominated officer, sometimes called a whistleblowing officer, whom you can approach confidentially, particularly if your manager is involved. If you have raised a concern and you are not satisfied with the response, you can take it to the Civil Service Commission. Laws such as the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protect workers who make certain disclosures in the public interest from detriment. Good practice is to state what you saw, when, and who may be involved, without guessing at motive. You do not need proof. You should not investigate by yourself, search other people's files, or confront the person, because that can alert them, damage evidence or breach rules on access to information. Going straight to the media or social media is usually a poor first step, because it bypasses the channels that can act. Worked example: you notice that payments are going to a supplier with no contract. You write down what you saw and tell your manager or nominated officer. Avoid dismissing it as none of your business, or acting like a detective.

questions.prompt: You notice a manager repeatedly approving payments to a supplier that appears to have no contract. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Confront the manager in front of the team
Search the manager's files and emails for evidence before you say anything to anyone at all
Write down what you saw and raise it with your line manager or the nominated officer
Post a description of the payments on a staff forum to see who else has noticed

questions.hint: Report facts through the proper channel and do not investigate yourself.

questions.prompt: The person you would normally report to is the one you believe is involved. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Discuss it with the person to hear their side first
Wait to see if the problem stops without action
Tell colleagues, so that they can keep an eye out
Use the nominated officer or another senior manager instead

questions.hint: The Code and department policies provide alternatives when the line manager is involved.

questions.prompt: You raised a concern two months ago and have heard nothing. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Drop it, since the department must have decided there was nothing in it
Ask colleagues to sign a joint complaint to put more pressure on the department
Ask for an update, and if still unsatisfied, consider the Civil Service Commission
Send the details to a newspaper, as that will force the department to reply

questions.hint: The Code allows escalation to the Commission when you are not satisfied.

questions.prompt: A colleague tells you privately about a possible fraud and asks you to keep it secret. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say you cannot promise secrecy, encourage them to report, and do so yourself if they will not
Keep it to yourself unless you see it happen again yourself
Raise it quietly with a few trusted team members to get their view first
Promise to keep it secret but advise them to report it when they feel ready

questions.hint: The duty to report cannot be set aside by a promise of secrecy.

questions.prompt: You suspect a colleague is inflating their timesheets. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Report what you have observed to your manager
Note down dates and details of what you saw
Ask the nominated officer how to proceed
Quietly copy their records and check them yourself before telling anyone

questions.hint: Investigating on your own may breach access rules and prejudice a proper inquiry.

questions.prompt: You are worried about something but are not sure you have understood it correctly. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask a friend outside work to say if it sounds wrong
Raise it anyway, explaining what you saw and what you do not know
Wait until you have gathered all the evidence yourself and can prove it
Say nothing at all, in case you have made a mistake and look foolish

questions.hint: You do not need certainty or proof to raise a concern in good faith.

questions.prompt: A minister's office gives an instruction that you believe may be improper. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Raise it with a senior official or the nominated officer, as the Code allows
Ignore the instruction and say nothing
Leak the instruction to a journalist
Carry out the instruction, as ministers decide policy

questions.hint: The Code provides routes for raising doubts about improper instructions.

questions.prompt: A colleague who raised a concern is now being excluded from meetings. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Advise them to withdraw the concern quietly to avoid more trouble
Stay out of it, since you had no part in the original concern
Support them, suggest they keep a record, and report the treatment through the proper route
Confront the manager involved on their behalf in front of others

questions.hint: Detriment for raising a concern should itself be reported.

questions.prompt: You have raised a concern and are asked not to discuss it with anyone while it is looked into. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Keep the matter confidential and wait for the outcome
Ask who you may talk to for support
Keep a private note of what you reported and when
Tell the rest of your team what you have reported so they can support you

questions.hint: Spreading details can harm the inquiry and the people involved.

items.title: L6: Political impartiality and serving the government of the day
items.source: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Management Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Impartiality means carrying out your role in a way that deserves and retains the confidence of ministers, while behaving in a way that would deserve the confidence of future governments. Civil servants serve the government of the day, whichever party it is, give honest and impartial advice, and do not use official resources for party political purposes. The Code also expects you to act in a way that is not influenced by your own political views, and to avoid undermining the political impartiality of the Civil Service. Civil servants are free to hold private political views, but the rules on political activity depend on grade and role: junior grades are generally free to take part in political activity, with restrictions, while more senior and sensitive roles are more limited. You should check the rules and ask permission before standing for election. Official information, such as policy options not yet decided, is not shared for political reasons. Special advisers are temporary civil servants appointed by ministers and can request advice but cannot direct civil servants to do party political work. Social media use should not suggest bias on matters you work on. Worked example: a minister from a different party takes office and asks for a briefing on the previous government's policy. You give an accurate and balanced account, and you do not editorialise.

questions.prompt: A new minister from a different party asks you for a briefing on the previous government's policy. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Highlight the policy's failings in your briefing, to please the new minister
Provide an accurate, balanced account of the policy and its results without editorialising
Decline until the briefing has been checked with the previous minister
Defend the policy strongly, since you worked hard on it yourself

questions.hint: You serve the government of the day, and your advice must be honest and impartial.

questions.prompt: A colleague posts strongly partisan comments on social media about a policy they work on. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Report them to the press office straight away
Say nothing, because it is their private account and their own business
Reply publicly to their post to correct their views
Tell them privately that this could breach the Code and suggest they stop

questions.hint: Visible partisanship on work matters can undermine confidence in impartiality.

questions.prompt: A special adviser asks you to draft a party political press release. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that party political work is not a civil service task and refer the request to your manager
Draft it, as special advisers are part of the Civil Service
Draft it outside office hours on your own laptop so that no official time is used
Draft it, but take out any reference to the department or your grade

questions.hint: Civil servants do not do party political work, even when asked by special advisers.

questions.prompt: You disagree with a policy but are asked to prepare options for it. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Raise your disagreement with your manager through the proper route
Weaken the options for the policy in your draft, so that ministers reconsider
Give your honest professional view in the advice
Present all the options fairly, including strengths and weaknesses

questions.hint: Advice must be objective, not shaped by your personal views.

questions.prompt: A neighbour who is a local councillor asks for an update on a decision your team has not yet announced. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say the decision is likely to be favourable
Share it in confidence, if the councillor promises to say nothing
Decline to share anything that is not public, as you would for anyone else
Share the outline of the decision, as the councillor is an elected representative

questions.hint: Non-public information is shared on a need-to-know basis, not because of someone's position.

questions.prompt: You are thinking of standing as a candidate in local elections. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Check the political activity rules for your grade and speak to HR first
Stand, since local elections are separate from central government
Stand under a different name to avoid any issue with your employer
Stand, and tell your manager only if you are elected

questions.hint: Political activity is restricted according to grade and role, and permission may be needed.

questions.prompt: A member of the public complains that you are not on their side in a dispute over a benefit decision. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Suggest they write to their MP to put pressure on the department
Stay polite, explain that decisions follow the rules and evidence, and describe how to appeal
Say that you personally agree with them but are bound by the rules
End the call and note them on the file as a difficult claimant

questions.hint: Impartial service means applying rules fairly and without taking sides.

questions.prompt: An MP's office contacts you about a constituent's case. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Refuse to respond, as MPs should not contact officials directly about cases
Prioritise the case over others in the queue, as the MP has asked
Handle it under the department's process, giving only information that is appropriate
Pass the MP's request to the minister's private office without any comment

questions.hint: Representations from MPs are handled through proper procedures, with no special treatment.

questions.prompt: You see a colleague wearing a party campaign badge in the office. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask other colleagues what they think before deciding whether to act
Ignore it, as people are free to hold their own opinions at work
Report them to the permanent secretary as a serious breach
Have a quiet word, explaining that visible party signs at work could undermine impartiality

questions.hint: Private views are allowed, but displaying them at work can affect public confidence.
